title: Attention
hook: attention is a form of love
tomorrow: what does washing your face have to do with fasting?

segments.voice: Yesterday, anger online: behind every screen, a person reads it. Today, the person who isn't behind a screen at all, the one sitting right next to you.

Your friend is telling you something that matters to her, and your thumb is still scrolling. You catch every third word. She trails off: never mind, it's nothing. So can full attention be a way to love someone? Mark's Gospel has a scene that runs the other way. A man runs up to Jesus on the road, kneels in the dust, and asks what he must do to have eternal life. Jesus is on his way somewhere. He could answer over his shoulder and keep walking. He stops.
screen: `EVERY THIRD WORD.` → `NEVER MIND, IT'S NOTHING.` → `A MAN KNEELS ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First Jesus lists the commandments: do not kill, do not steal, honor your father and mother. The man says he has kept them all since he was young. A good man, then, and an honest one, and he still came running down the road, because something was missing and he knew it. Jesus could have praised him and moved on. Then comes a line Mark didn't have to write. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And Jesus looking on him, loved him." The look comes first, and the love is inside it. Only then does Jesus say the hard thing: one thing is missing; sell what you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me. And the man goes away sad, because he had great possessions. Here's something to tell a friend tonight: Matthew and Luke tell this same story, and neither one includes that line. Mark keeps it. And Mark never says the love was taken back when the man walked off. The love didn't wait for the right answer. That's the Catholic case for attention. A gaze that stays on a person, without rushing to the next thing, is already a kind of love, whatever they decide. Pope Francis says the same about family life in Amoris Laetitia: love takes time, and it means listening patiently and attentively to everything the other person wants to say, without jumping in to fix it.
screen: `LOOKING ON HIM, LOVED HIM.` · `THEN THE HARD THING.` · `MATTHEW AND LUKE LEAVE IT OUT.` · `LISTEN PATIENTLY, ATTENTIVELY.` · then, large: `ATTENTION IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: If someone is near you, turn toward them and listen to one whole sentence without planning your reply. If you're alone, open a photo of one face you love and simply look at it for the whole sit, the way Jesus looked at the man on the road, with nowhere else to be. When your mind runs ahead to the next thing, notice it, and bring your eyes back.
Attention. Keeping your eyes on a person, not on the next thing. Today's word.
Your line: attention is love. In Mark, the look came before the hard words. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics practice attention in prayer and in the moments of silence at Mass, and at home; Pope Francis's letter on family love, Amoris Laetitia, names patient, attentive listening as part of love.

fork.setup: your little brother holds up a drawing while you're mid-reply in a group chat. going by Mark's order, what comes first?
options: finish the reply, then give him a really good compliment.
put the phone down and look at him and the drawing.
say "so cool!" right away so he doesn't feel ignored.
fork.reveal: in Mark, the look comes before any words: looking on him, Jesus loved him. a fast compliment can still skip the look.

chat.meaning: In Mark, Jesus looked at the man and loved him before saying anything. The attention itself is the gift.
